changes.local: In the case of banked curves, where the slope of the road helps you negotiate the curve, some or all of the necessary centripetal force is provided by the normal force. See . The greater the angle [MATH] , the faster you can take the curve. Race tracks for bikes as well as cars, for example, often have steeply banked curves. In an “ideally banked curve,” the angle [MATH] is such that you can negotiate the curve at a certain speed without the aid of friction between the tires and the road. Conceptually, for ideal banking, the net external force equals the horizontal centripetal force in the absence of friction. The components of the normal force [MATH] in the horizontal and vertical directions must equal the centripetal force and the weight of the car, respectively.
